source.title: Beyond Attack Success Rate: Temporal Logit Observability for LLM Safety Failures
source.authors: Junyoung Park; Sunghwan Park; S. Ju; Jaewook Lee

record.tranche_reason: The study uses a harmful-minus-benign hidden-state direction as a validation reference for its logit diagnostic and reports their alignment. It does not intervene on that direction or test whether it causally mediates refusal.
record.gate_note: The study constructs and measures a difference-of-means hidden-state direction, then compares its projections with logit trajectories. It reports no direction ablation, addition, or weight edit. The TLO behavioral probe and its ASR results concern the study's own early-stop rule, not removal or addition of the refusal direction, so they are not rows for these claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study builds a per-model harmful-minus-benign difference-of-means direction at a fixed mid layer. It uses that direction only as a construct-validity reference for its logit-margin diagnostic, reporting the correlation between direction projections and the logit margin. It never ablates, adds, or weight-edits the direction, and it does not measure refusal rates as a function of the direction. The early-stop ASR results come from the study's own halt rule. The direction-alignment results are therefore the study's own method validated against a cited tool, not a test of whether the direction mediates refusal.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that TLO separates conditions with similar ASR, that its trajectory aligns with hidden-state refusal-direction projections in 10 of 12 conditions (Qwen is the boundary case, attributed to the fixed lexicon), and that a tcross early-stop rule cuts ASR from 39.6% to 13.1%. They explicitly say TLO is observational and does not identify causal mechanisms.
record.recipe_differences: The study computes a per-model harmful-minus-benign hidden-state direction at a fixed layer and measures its temporal association with a compliance–refusal logit margin. It does not apply the original refusal-direction ablation or addition intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: Alignment varies by model and attack: Llama has strong alignment across its attacks; Qwen includes reversed-sign associations; Mistral and Gemma show weaker or moderate associations depending on attack. The study also reports layer-sweep results at L25, L50, and L75.

fits_no_version.finding: A logit-level compliance–refusal margin computed from a fixed lexicon tracks decoding-time projections onto a difference-of-means harmful-minus-benign direction. The expected negative sign appears in 10 of 12 model–attack conditions. Llama is strong (|ρ| about 0.70–0.79), Mistral and Gemma are weak to moderate, and Qwen reverses sign under MCM and DI.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Output-logit refusal/compliance margins co-vary over time with the hidden-state refusal direction, with strength depending on the model.

record.code_released: Supplementary archive includes code and reproduction scripts; URL not stated
record.problems: The direction comparison is observational and does not establish causal mediation. The direction is constructed from harmful-versus-benign references, which the authors note may also encode harmful-versus-benign context. The fixed English lexicon and Llama-Guard primary success labels have stated scope limitations; auxiliary judges show some condition-level disagreements.
record.rows_left_out: TLO RP coordinates, jailbreak ASR/AUC results, and early-stop intervention results are omitted because they do not measure an intervention on the refusal direction or its predicted causal effects. Other supplementary diagnostics are likewise outside the direction-alignment finding recorded here.

untested.parts: Ablation removing refusal, addition inducing refusal, and capability preservation; no interventions on the direction.

Projections are recorded under jailbreaks (MCM, GCG, DI), but no comparison of projection suppression between successful and failed attacks is reported, and there is no adversarial training against ablation.
The direction is noted to possibly encode harmful-versus-benign context, but harm and refusal are not separated.
Directions are built per model; no transfer test.

record.verdict_notes: The study cites Arditi et al. [1] and adopts the direction construction as a reference tool. The layer sweep (Table 15: L25/L50/L75) shows the alignment is not tuned to one layer, but it is still method validation. The record's reader guesses (uses_without_test, T4, no labels) are confirmed.

versions.untested_parts: Causal mediation; ablation and addition effects on refusal; preservation of general capability.
No refusal-direction weight edit or abliteration.
No test of attacks suppressing the direction or training against its ablation.
No comparison of a single direction with an affine, cone, or multiple-direction account.
No separation of harmfulness judgment from refusal decision.
Directions are constructed per model; no cross-language, cross-variant, or base-to-instruct transfer test.
No comparison of refusal-training methods or timing.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Project decoding-time hidden states onto a per-model harmful-minus-benign difference-of-means direction at L50 and compare with the LMS trajectory.
rows.measure: Temporal association between LMS and hidden-state direction projection
rows.value: |ρ|₀:₄ = 0.698; signed ρ̄₀:₄ = -0.698; lag-optimized similarity = 0.599; state-sign agreement = 0.758
rows.note: The paper treats this as an observational alignment measure, not a causal test of the direction.
rows.check: This is an observational correlation between the paper's own logit metric and the direction projection, used to validate its method. It is not a measure of refusal mediation. Linking it to no version is correct.
